title: AI Sales Lead Engine
summary: Turns Arabic sales inquiries from three channels into one ranked HubSpot queue. Each lead carries a reason for its priority.
overview: A property buyer can fill in a form, message an agent in Arabic and change their budget before anyone calls back. I built a workflow that keeps those conversations together and gives a salesperson a reason to make the next call.
problem: An inquiry that arrives twice can become two deals. A colloquial budget or a request to be called later can also disappear when the conversation moves between channels.
audience: Real-estate sales representatives who need to decide which buyer to contact next.
contribution: I connected lead intake to HubSpot, implemented scoring rules in Python and JavaScript, and tested both versions on the same inputs.
solution: The language model proposes field values with quotes from the buyer. Code checks each quote, parses the budget and calculates priority before the workflow updates the CRM.

architecture.title: Collect
architecture.detail: Form, Meta and WhatsApp webhooks receive inquiries.

architecture.title: Reconcile
architecture.detail: Normalize contact details and match repeat events.

architecture.title: Qualify
architecture.detail: Check Arabic extractions and apply budget and priority rules.

architecture.title: Queue
architecture.detail: Update the HubSpot contact and deal, then export the ranked callback list.

tradeoff: Two implementations of the rules let me test in Python and run inside n8n Cloud. A parity test checks that the JavaScript port reaches the same decision.
reliability: A replayed event is ignored once its CRM update succeeds. Uncertain budgets go to review. Offline scenarios cover duplicate leads, revised budgets, existing contacts and requests for a person.
future: I would test simultaneous updates to the same lead and expand the Arabic budget fixtures with reviewed, synthetic examples.
evidence: Public project README, rules and parity test at commit 8759a6d.
The committed offline scenario log uses simulated CRM calls and model outputs.

title: Multilingual RAG Assistant
summary: Searches a collection of question-and-answer passages, reranks close matches and checks whether the retrieved text can support an answer.
outcome: Retrieved the expected passage first for 80 of 100 paraphrased questions.
overview: A search system can look accurate when people repeat the wording in its index. I built this question-answering API and measured what happened when the same questions were asked in different words.
problem: Similar passages compete for first place. Reranking every query adds latency and can reorder an already strong match.
audience: Developers evaluating retrieval quality before adding a question-answering API to an application.
contribution: I built the indexing pipeline, added confidence-gated reranking and exposed the retrieval and generation stages through FastAPI. I compared verbatim questions and paraphrases on the same sample.
solution: FAISS searches question-and-answer text embedded with a multilingual encoder. When the top scores are close, a cross-encoder reranks the candidates. The response can answer, surface a passage or decline.

architecture.title: Index
architecture.detail: Clean and embed each question with its answer passage.

architecture.title: Retrieve
architecture.detail: Search the FAISS index and compare the top two scores.

architecture.title: Rerank
architecture.detail: Rescore close candidates against the same question-and-answer representation.

architecture.title: Respond
architecture.detail: Ground the reply in the retrieved text and record the request by session.

tradeoff: Reranking answer text alone pushed correct matches down the list. Matching the index representation and reserving reranking for close calls restored two documented regressions.
reliability: The evaluation uses the original passage ID as its target. On 100 paired questions, rank-one retrieval fell from 95 verbatim matches to 80 paraphrased matches. Near-duplicate passages can make this measure stricter than a reader's judgment.
future: I would add human judgments for equivalent passages and a separate multilingual query set to test the encoder beyond the existing English evaluation.
evidence: Public README and paired paraphrase evaluation at commit 262d844. The result measures passage retrieval on the project's sample.

title: Real-time Voice AI
summary: Connects streaming audio, GPU speech processing and Azure OpenAI to support a live spoken conversation.
outcome: Deployed a working speech-to-speech system at Neqabty.
overview: A voice interface has to listen and respond while the person is still engaged. At Neqabty, I built and deployed a real-time system for spoken interactions.
problem: The time spent transporting audio, processing speech and producing a response is felt as one pause by the speaker.
audience: People using a spoken support interface and the engineers integrating it with the client application.
contribution: I connected WebSocket streaming to the Azure OpenAI Realtime API and GPU-accelerated speech services on A100 infrastructure.
solution: The system carries audio over a persistent connection and brings together speech recognition, conversational inference and synthesis. The diagram groups the documented components by their purpose.

architecture.title: Audio stream
architecture.detail: WebSockets carry live audio between the client and service.

architecture.title: Speech and dialogue
architecture.detail: GPU speech services and Azure OpenAI Realtime process the conversation.

architecture.title: Spoken reply
architecture.detail: The response returns to the user as audio.

tradeoff: A persistent connection supports interactive audio. It also makes interrupted sessions and network delays part of the user experience.
reliability: The engineering question is whether the full conversation feels responsive. A representative test would include transport, turn detection and output audio as well as model processing.
future: I would publish an approval-cleared demo and a latency distribution with explicit measurement points and network conditions.
evidence: Mohamed Ibrahim’s supplied CV, page 1, Neqabty AI Engineer. Deployment and stack are résumé-reported. A public benchmark and recording were unavailable.

title: Arabic Document Search
summary: Helps syndicate users find answers inside Arabic PDFs. Each response points back to the passages used to produce it.
outcome: Deployed across five syndicates, as reported in my CV.
overview: Finding the right paragraph in a collection of Arabic PDFs can take longer than answering the question itself. At Neqabty, I designed a retrieval system that brings source passages into the conversation.
problem: Users need to verify an answer against the original document. A plausible response is difficult to trust when they cannot locate its source.
audience: Users of syndicate services searching information held in Arabic documents.
contribution: I architected the Azure retrieval system, built custom embedding pipelines and worked with the backend and mobile teams on delivery.
solution: Document Intelligence extracts text, an embedding pipeline makes passages searchable, and Azure AI Search supplies relevant context to GPT-4o for a cited response.

architecture.title: Extract
architecture.detail: Read the Arabic PDFs with Azure AI Document Intelligence.

architecture.title: Index
architecture.detail: Represent passages with embeddings and index them in Azure AI Search.

architecture.title: Retrieve
architecture.detail: Find relevant passages for the user's question.

architecture.title: Cite
architecture.detail: Generate a response grounded in the retrieved material.

tradeoff: The answer depends on the quality of both text extraction and search. A citation makes the supporting text available for a reader to inspect.
reliability: Useful evaluation cases include imperfect PDF extraction, a question with several plausible passages and a question the documents cannot answer. Client documents and example queries stay private.
future: I would build an Arabic evaluation set from material cleared for publication and score passage retrieval separately from citation accuracy.
evidence: Mohamed Ibrahim’s supplied CV, page 1, Neqabty AI Engineer. The CV reports deployment across five syndicates and over 1,000 monthly queries.

title: Retail Analytics Copilot
summary: Answers retail questions using policy documents and Northwind sales data. A LangGraph workflow selects retrieval, SQL or both.
outcome: Five of six questions answered correctly in the documented evaluation.
overview: “How long can a customer return a beverage?” needs a policy. “Which category sold the most during a campaign?” needs a date range and a calculation. I built a local copilot that can take either path.
problem: Business definitions live in documents while sales figures live in tables. A query can execute successfully and still answer the wrong business question.
audience: Analysts exploring how a local language model could combine policy lookups with sales calculations.
contribution: I implemented the agent graph, added worked SQL examples for the local model and reconciled campaign dates with the sample database.
solution: The graph routes each question to document search, SQLite or a hybrid flow. For hybrid questions, retrieved definitions and dates guide SQL generation. Results include the answer and its source documents or tables.

architecture.title: Route
architecture.detail: Select a document, SQL or hybrid path.

architecture.title: Plan
architecture.detail: Retrieve policy text and campaign constraints when needed.

architecture.title: Execute
architecture.detail: Generate SQL and retry a failed statement up to twice.

architecture.title: Synthesize
architecture.detail: Format a typed answer with citations to documents or tables.

tradeoff: A small local model kept inference on the machine but needed worked examples for SQLite joins and dates. The campaign calendar also had to agree with the years in Northwind.
reliability: In the six-question evaluation, an all-time ranking returned no rows because the planner added an irrelevant campaign date. The saved output exposes the SQL so the error can be traced.
future: I would protect all-time questions against inherited date filters and test the planner on a larger held-out set with read-only database access.
evidence: Public project README, saved evaluation output and agent graph at commit 8b43042. The six-question result applies to the project's sample database.

title: BOKRANA
summary: An Arabic learning platform where beginners apply generative AI in live sessions and submit a practical project for instructor review.
outcome: A live four-week course with eight scheduled sessions and a capstone submission path.
overview: BOKRANA gives Arabic-speaking beginners a route from a practical question to a project they can share. The public course and private student dashboard connect the lessons, enrollment and final project.
problem: A list of AI tools gives a learner little guidance on how to use them in a real assignment. The course uses practical work and instructor feedback to connect individual sessions.
audience: Arabic-speaking students, teachers and professionals learning to use generative AI in their work.
contribution: I teach the generative AI course and review submitted projects. The curriculum covers research, content creation, presentations and website building.
solution: The platform explains enrollment, takes learners through a four-week course and accepts their capstone through the student dashboard. Learners can opt to submit work for the public showcase.

architecture.title: Explore
architecture.detail: Read the public syllabus and choose a practical goal.

architecture.title: Enroll
architecture.detail: Sign in and complete the payment-review process.

architecture.title: Build
architecture.detail: Apply the live sessions to a final project.

architecture.title: Review
architecture.detail: Submit the project for instructor review and optional publication.

tradeoff: Reviewing payment and project submissions adds a manual step. It gives the instructor control over access and which work is made public.
reliability: Course access begins after payment approval. Public examples are labeled separately from student work, and the showcase describes the instructor review required before publication.
future: I would publish an opt-in capstone walkthrough that documents the learner's question, tool choices, revisions and final result.
evidence: BOKRANA public instructor profile, course syllabus, enrollment instructions and project showcase reviewed on 25 November 2026. The diagram describes the learner journey.
